title: US hits Iranian air-defence site on Qeshm again as Qatar pushes two-day deal
dek: Trump said US forces 'knocked out' an anti-aircraft device in minutes. Qatar's plan would swap the end of the US port blockade for a reopened Strait of Hormuz.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
US forces struck an Iranian air-defence site on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz early on Saturday, the second such strike on the island this week, as Qatar pressed both sides to accept a two-day "bridge" deal that would lift the US blockade of Iranian ports in exchange for reopening the strait.

President Donald Trump confirmed the action to reporters in Florida on Friday evening, US time, describing it as limited and minor. "They built a little bit of an anti-aircraft device and we knocked it out in about 15 minutes, maybe five," he said, according to reports. In the same remarks he said Washington was "talking to Iran" and was "doing very well" with Tehran.

## What happened

Iranian state media reported two explosions in the Suza area of Qeshm, the largest island in the strait, in the early hours of Saturday. One state news agency said local witnesses heard an aircraft before two projectiles struck; another said two missiles had hit the island. Iranian authorities have not released any damage assessment or casualty figures, and the link between the impacts and the US operation has not been independently established.

Hours earlier, Iranian media citing the Revolutionary Guards said air defences had destroyed a US MQ-1 Predator drone over Qeshm on Friday night. The United States has not commented on that claim, and it cannot be independently verified. On Friday the Guards had also claimed to have shot down two US reconnaissance drones over the island.

The US military did not issue a separate statement on the strike. Late on Friday, US Central Command posted an offer on X of a reward of up to $20 million, and possible relocation, for information about Iran's nuclear programme, according to reports.

This is the second US strike on Qeshm in a week. US officials described earlier strikes on Qeshm and Hengam islands and around Bandar Abbas, carried out at the start of the week, as "defensive" action against surface-to-air missile systems that had been used against US aircraft, and said they did not mark a return to major combat. Reports differ on whether those strikes took place on Monday or Tuesday.

## Qatar's two-day plan

Qatar, the chief mediator, has put a sequenced proposal to both governments, according to reports citing people familiar with it. On the first day, the US would lift its blockade of Iranian ports and release some frozen Iranian funds, and Iran would let inspectors from the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) into sites hit by US and Israeli strikes. On the second day, Iran would reopen the Strait of Hormuz under a temporary arrangement with Oman, pending a permanent deal involving other Gulf states. Wider US-Iran talks on Iran's stockpile of highly enriched uranium would follow.

The Oman arrangement in the plan is a modified version of an Iran-Oman agreement that Washington has not approved, reports said. The White House declined to comment on the Qatari proposals. Qatar's International Media Office denied reports that the negotiations had collapsed.

Qatar's Prime Minister, Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani, urged the two sides to reach a deal rather than wait for a "perfect moment", according to reports. Mr Trump spoke to Qatar's emir by phone this week, and US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth spoke to Qatar's defence minister, Sheikh Saoud bin Abdulrahman Al Thani.

## What Iran is demanding

Iranian officials say Tehran will not begin nuclear negotiations until the United States meets a set of conditions: ending the blockade of its ports, lifting sanctions, releasing frozen assets, paying compensation for war damage and ending hostilities in the region, including Israeli operations in Lebanon. A senior Iranian official said talks could start only once those conditions were met, according to reports.

Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has kept up calls around the region, speaking this week to his counterparts in Iraq, Tunisia, Egypt, Saudi Arabia and the UAE. Iran's army has warned that renewed US attacks would bring retaliation against American military assets beyond the Middle East.

## Background

The United States and Iran have been in conflict for most of 2026, and the Strait of Hormuz, through which a large share of the world's seaborne oil normally passes, has been largely closed to traffic Tehran does not approve. Iran has let ships linked to some countries, including India, China, Qatar and Iraq, pass under exemptions, while the US has blockaded Iranian ports. The IAEA says Iran holds 440.9 kg of uranium enriched to 60%, a short technical step from weapons grade; Iran says its programme is peaceful.

Attacks on shipping have continued. The UK Maritime Trade Operations centre recorded at least 30 attacks on commercial vessels in the region in October, a record, according to reports. On Thursday a seafarer was killed in an explosion believed to have been caused by a missile on the empty tanker Velos Sapphire, bound for Bahrain, its Greek manager said. No one has said who fired at the ship.

The war has also shaped US politics. Republicans lost control of Congress in Tuesday's midterm elections, and Vice-President JD Vance said "the reason we lost is the war", according to reports. Mr Trump said that was "largely true" because the war had pushed up petrol prices. Oil prices have eased on hopes of a deal: Brent crude fell below $100 a barrel this week for the first time since early October, after peaking near $118 at the end of October.

## Why it matters for India

India buys most of its crude oil and liquefied gas from the Gulf, and much of it normally travels through Hormuz. A deal that reopens the strait would ease freight and insurance costs for Indian importers and lower the risk to the many Indian seafarers working on tankers in the Gulf; a return to full-scale war would do the opposite. Millions of Indians live and work in the Gulf states, where airlines are still cancelling flights. This week the US Treasury also sanctioned a network that it said was run by two Indian nationals and helped Iran's "shadow fleet" of tankers with false flags and fake certificates, according to reports.

## What happens next

Washington has not said whether it accepts the Qatari sequence. Iran says it will not reopen the strait fully until its conditions are met. Mr Trump has said he will decide soon whether to resume large-scale strikes, and Gulf mediators are expected to keep shuttling between the two sides over the weekend.

## Key numbers

- 2: US strikes on Qeshm Island this week, by US and Iranian accounts
- 440.9 kg: Iran's stock of 60% enriched uranium, according to the IAEA
- 30+: attacks on merchant ships in the region in October, according to reports
- $20 million: reward offered by US Central Command for information on Iran's nuclear programme
